content: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall lack nothing. {{v:2}} He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters. {{v:3}} He restores my soul. He guides me in the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake. {{v:4}} Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me. Your rod and your staff, they comfort me. {{v:5}} You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies. You anoint my head with oil. My cup runs over. {{v:6}} Surely goodness and loving kindness shall follow me all the days of my life, and I will dwell in the LORD’s house forever.

facets.text: The psalm opens by naming the LORD as "my shepherd," a confession that grounds the whole prayer in a personal covenant relationship. Because God shepherds, the psalmist "shall lack nothing" — not a promise of wealth but of sufficiency in God himself, who provides rest, water, and restoration of the soul. The imagery of green pastures and still waters portrays divine care that both sustains life and gives peace.
facets.question: What does it mean to say the Lord is my shepherd?

facets.text: God's guidance "in the paths of righteousness" is undertaken "for his name's sake," meaning the shepherd leads not merely for the sheep's benefit but for the glory and faithfulness of his own name. This roots the believer's moral life in God's initiative rather than human merit; righteousness is a path we are led into, not one we blaze ourselves. The restoration of the soul and the guidance in righteousness together reveal salvation as God's work.
facets.question: Why does God lead us in righteous paths for his own name's sake?

facets.text: "Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me" marks a turning point where the psalm shifts from speaking about God to speaking directly to him. The remedy for fear is not the absence of danger but the presence of God — a truth fulfilled in Emmanuel, "God with us." The rod and staff, instruments of both protection and correction, comfort precisely because they signify the shepherd's active nearness.
facets.question: How can I face death and danger without fear?

facets.text: The image shifts from shepherd to host: God "prepares a table" and "anoints the head with oil" while enemies look on, so that the believer feasts securely in the very presence of hostility. The overflowing cup expresses abundance beyond need. Catholic tradition has long read this table and anointing as prefiguring the Eucharistic banquet and the sacramental anointing that mark the life of grace.
facets.question: What is the meaning of the prepared table and the overflowing cup in Psalm 23?

facets.text: The psalm closes with confidence that "goodness and loving kindness shall follow me all the days of my life," portraying God's mercy not as something chased after but as a companion pursuing the believer from behind. The final hope, to "dwell in the LORD's house forever," reaches beyond earthly life toward eternal communion with God. This makes Psalm 23 a prayer of enduring trust that culminates in the hope of heaven.
facets.question: What is the final hope expressed at the end of Psalm 23?

facets.text: Read in the light of the New Testament, the shepherd of this psalm is fulfilled in Jesus Christ, who declares himself the Good Shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep. The valley of the shadow of death and the table in the presence of enemies find their deepest meaning in Christ's passion and the Eucharist he leaves his Church. Thus the whole psalm becomes a portrait of the believer's life under Christ's care, from grace through death to glory.
facets.question: How does Jesus fulfill the shepherd of Psalm 23?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: Psalm 23 confesses the LORD as shepherd and host who provides, guides, protects through death, feasts the believer amid enemies, and brings him to dwell in God's house forever; Catholic tradition reads it Christologically and Eucharistically.

[SCRIPTURAL | explicit]: The LORD as personal shepherd means the believer lacks nothing, receiving rest, still waters, and restoration of soul as sufficiency in God himself.
[DOCTRINAL | traditional]: God guides into paths of righteousness "for his name's sake," grounding the moral and saved life in divine initiative rather than human merit.
[DEVOTIONAL | explicit]: The remedy for fear in the valley of death's shadow is God's presence, not absence of danger; the rod and staff comfort as signs of the shepherd's nearness, fulfilled in Emmanuel.
[TYPOLOGICAL | traditional]: The prepared table, anointing with oil, and overflowing cup signify abundant grace and prefigure the Eucharistic banquet and sacramental anointing.
[DEVOTIONAL | inferential]: Goodness and mercy pursue the believer all his days, and dwelling in the LORD's house forever expresses the hope of eternal communion and heaven.
[TYPOLOGICAL | traditional]: Christ the Good Shepherd fulfills the psalm, with the death-valley and enemy-table pointing to his passion and Eucharist, mapping the believer's journey from grace through death to glory.

content: They compelled one passing by, coming from the country, Simon of Cyrene, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to go with them that he might bear his cross. {{v:22}} They brought him to the place called Golgotha, which is, being interpreted, “The place of a skull.” {{v:23}} They offered him wine mixed with myrrh to drink, but he didn’t take it. {{v:24}} Crucifying him, they parted his garments among them, casting lots on them, what each should take. {{v:25}} It was the third hour when they crucified him. {{v:26}} The superscription of his accusation was written over him: “THE KING OF THE JEWS.” {{v:27}} With him they crucified two robbers, one on his right hand, and one on his left. {{v:28}} The Scripture was fulfilled which says, “He was counted with transgressors.” {{v:29}} Those who passed by blasphemed him, wagging their heads and saying, “Ha! You who destroy the temple and build it in three days, {{v:30}} save yourself, and come down from the cross!” {{v:31}} Likewise, also the chief priests mocking among themselves with the scribes said, “He saved others. He can’t save himself. {{v:32}} Let the Christ, the King of Israel, now come down from the cross, that we may see and believe him.” Those who were crucified with him also insulted him. {{v:33}} When the sixth hour had come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour. {{v:34}} At the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, “Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?” which is, being interpreted, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” {{v:35}} Some of those who stood by, when they heard it, said, “Behold, he is calling Elijah.” {{v:36}} One ran, and filling a sponge full of vinegar, put it on a reed and gave it to him to drink, saying, “Let him be. Let’s see whether Elijah comes to take him down.” {{v:37}} Jesus cried out with a loud voice, and gave up the spirit. {{v:38}} The veil of the temple was torn in two from the top to the bottom. {{v:39}} When the centurion, who stood by opposite him, saw that he cried out like this and breathed his last, he said, “Truly this man was the Son of God!” {{v:40}} There were also women watching from afar, among whom were both Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of James the less and of Joses, and Salome; {{v:41}} who, when he was in Galilee, followed him and served him; and many other women who came up with him to Jerusalem.

facets.text: Mark's crucifixion narrative is saturated with fulfilled Scripture: Jesus' garments are divided by casting lots (Psalm 22:18), he is offered vinegar to drink (Psalm 69:21), and he is reckoned among transgressors with the two robbers (Isaiah 53:12). The evangelist presents the cross not as the tragic collapse of Jesus' mission but as the deliberate accomplishment of God's plan foretold in the Law and Prophets. Even the mockery and abandonment fulfill the pattern of the suffering righteous one.
facets.question: How does Jesus' crucifixion fulfill the Old Testament prophecies?

facets.text: Jesus' cry, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" quotes the opening line of Psalm 22, a lament that moves from anguish to vindication and universal praise. Far from despair, this invocation places Christ's suffering within the prayer of the righteous sufferer who ultimately trusts and is delivered by God. In taking this psalm on his lips, Jesus enters fully into the depths of human abandonment while remaining in filial relationship with the Father.
facets.question: What did Jesus mean when he cried out that God had forsaken him?

facets.text: The tearing of the temple veil from top to bottom, occurring at the moment of Jesus' death, signifies that the barrier separating God from humanity has been removed by his sacrifice. The direction—from top to bottom—indicates a divine act rather than a human one. Christ's death opens access to the Holy of Holies, and the old temple order gives way to the new worship inaugurated by his self-offering.
facets.question: What is the meaning of the temple veil tearing when Jesus died?

facets.text: The centurion's confession, "Truly this man was the Son of God," is the climactic human recognition in Mark's Gospel, and it comes from a Gentile who sees precisely how Jesus dies. What the disciples, crowds, and religious leaders failed to grasp, a pagan soldier confesses at the foot of the cross. This reveals that Christ's divine sonship is disclosed most fully in his suffering and death, and that faith is offered to all nations.
facets.question: Why is it significant that a Roman centurion recognized Jesus as the Son of God at the cross?

facets.text: The mockers unwittingly proclaim the truth: they taunt Jesus as the one who would "destroy the temple and build it in three days" and demand he save himself, while "He saved others; he cannot save himself." The irony is that Jesus does not come down precisely because he saves others—his refusal to save himself is the means of their salvation. The true temple he raises is his risen body, and his kingship is manifested through the cross, not by escaping it.
facets.question: Why did Jesus refuse to save himself from the cross when he had saved others?

facets.text: The mocking title placed over Jesus, "THE KING OF THE JEWS," proclaims a truth in derision that the whole scene fulfills. Enthroned on the cross with two crucified on his right and left, Jesus reigns not through worldly power but through suffering love. Mark presents the crucifixion itself as the paradoxical coronation of the Messiah.
facets.question: In what sense is Jesus truly a king while dying on the cross?

facets.text: While the male disciples have fled, the Gospel highlights the women who watched from afar—Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, and Salome—who had followed and served Jesus in Galilee. Their faithful presence at the cross and their prior discipleship of service model fidelity in the hour of trial. Mark thereby honors these women as true disciples and prepares them as the first witnesses to the empty tomb.
facets.question: Who remained faithful to Jesus at the cross when the disciples fled?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: Mark's account of the crucifixion and death of Jesus, presenting the cross as the scripturally foretold, saving self-offering of the Son of God and King, culminating in the torn temple veil, the centurion's confession, and the faithful witness of the women.

[SCRIPTURAL | traditional]: The dividing of garments, offered vinegar, and reckoning with transgressors fulfill Psalm 22, Psalm 69, and Isaiah 53, showing the cross as God's foretold plan.
[SCRIPTURAL | traditional]: Jesus' cry quotes Psalm 22, entering total human abandonment while remaining the trusting righteous sufferer in filial relationship to the Father.
[TYPOLOGICAL | traditional]: The temple veil torn top-to-bottom signals a divine act removing the barrier to God, opening access to the Holy of Holies through Christ's death.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: A Gentile centurion confesses Jesus as Son of God, the Gospel's climactic recognition, disclosed precisely in how Jesus suffers and dies.
[DOCTRINAL | inferential]: The mockers' taunts are unwitting truth—Jesus does not save himself because he saves others, raising the true temple of his risen body.
[TYPOLOGICAL | traditional]: The mocking title "King of the Jews" and crucifixion between two others present the cross as the Messiah's paradoxical enthronement.
[DEVOTIONAL | explicit]: The faithful women who followed and served Jesus remain at the cross while disciples flee, modeling fidelity and preparing to witness the tomb.
